meta.title: How the internet works
meta.description: Module 3 of Introduction to Computer Networks: what happens between typing a web address and seeing the page, in four short lessons.
meta.author: Northgate College, Department of Computing

summary: DNS turns a name such as `www.example.org` into an IP address by asking a chain of servers, and caches the answer. IP moves packets between networks on a best-effort basis, and TCP turns them into a reliable, ordered stream. HTTP is the language browser and server speak over that stream, and TLS wraps it so nobody in between can read or change it.

meta.question: How does my computer find the server behind a name?
meta.title: DNS: names to addresses

answer.headline: Your computer asks a recursive resolver, which asks a root server, then the top-level domain's server, then the domain's own authoritative server, and caches the answer for as long as its TTL allows.
answer.text: Computers route traffic by IP address, not by name. The Domain Name System is a distributed directory: no single server knows every name, but each knows who to ask next.
points: Most lookups are answered from a cache in milliseconds
A full lookup from scratch takes three or four round trips
DNS normally uses UDP port 53, and TCP for large answers

blocks.title: Why a DNS change takes time to appear
blocks.label: TTL
blocks.body: Every record carries a time to live in seconds. A resolver that cached a record with a TTL of 3600 keeps using the old address for up to an hour after you change it. Lower the TTL a day before a planned move.

meta.question: How do packets get to the server and arrive in order?
meta.title: TCP/IP: moving packets

answer.headline: IP carries each packet from network to network on a best-effort basis; TCP, running at both ends, numbers the bytes, resends what is lost and puts them back in order.
answer.text: The internet is a network of networks. Routers only look at the destination IP address and pass each packet one hop closer. They do not guarantee delivery, and packets can arrive late, twice or not at all.
points: IP addresses find the machine; port numbers find the program on it
TCP opens a connection with a three-way handshake before any data
UDP skips all of this: faster, but the application must cope with loss

blocks.title: The layers
rows: What the programs say to each other

Moving frames on one physical network

items.title: SYN
items.text: The client picks a random starting sequence number and asks to connect.

items.title: SYN-ACK
items.text: The server acknowledges it and sends its own starting number.

items.title: ACK
items.text: The client acknowledges the server's number. Both sides can now send data.

items.title: Sequence numbers
items.text: Every byte is numbered, so the receiver can reorder and spot gaps.

items.title: Acknowledgements
items.text: The receiver says what it has; anything unacknowledged is sent again.

items.title: Congestion control
items.text: The sender slows down when packets go missing, so the network is not overwhelmed.

options.name: TCP

pros: Late data can simply be skipped

items.q: How does a router know where to send a packet?
items.a: It looks up the destination address in its routing table and picks the most specific matching route. Between large networks, the tables are built by BGP, which networks use to announce which addresses they can reach.

items.q: Why are there two kinds of IP address?
items.a: IPv4 has about 4.3 billion addresses, which ran out. IPv6 uses 128-bit addresses, enough that every device can have its own. Most networks now run both.

meta.question: What do the browser and the server actually say to each other?
meta.title: HTTP: requests and responses

answer.headline: The browser sends a request naming a method and a path; the server sends back a status code, headers and a body. Every page is many of these exchanges, one for each file.
answer.text: HTTP is a request-response protocol. It is stateless: each request stands alone, and cookies are how a site remembers you between them.
points: A typical page makes 50 to 100 requests: HTML, styles, scripts, images
HTTP/2 sends them all over one connection at once
HTTP/3 runs over QUIC on UDP, so one lost packet no longer blocks the rest

meta.question: How does HTTPS keep the connection private?
meta.title: TLS: the padlock

answer.headline: TLS proves the server is who it claims with a certificate signed by a trusted authority, then both sides agree fresh encryption keys, so nobody in between can read or change the traffic.
answer.text: HTTPS is HTTP inside a TLS connection. TLS 1.3, published in 2018, needs only one round trip to set up and removes older, weaker options.
points: The certificate proves identity; the key exchange provides secrecy
Keys are new for every connection, so a stolen server key cannot unlock old recordings
The padlock means the connection is private, not that the site is honest

items.title: Client hello
items.text: The browser lists the ciphers it supports and sends its half of a Diffie-Hellman key exchange.

items.title: Server hello
items.text: The server picks a cipher, sends its half of the key exchange and, already encrypted, its certificate and a signature.

items.title: Check the certificate
items.text: The browser checks the name matches, the dates are valid and the chain leads to a certificate authority it trusts.

items.title: Finished
items.text: Both sides derive the same session keys. The first HTTP request goes straight after, encrypted.

items.title: Confidentiality
items.text: The content is encrypted. An observer still sees which IP address you connect to and roughly how much data moves.

items.title: Integrity
items.text: Any change to the data in transit is detected and the connection is dropped.

items.title: Authentication
items.text: The certificate shows you reached the real owner of the domain name.

blocks.title: The padlock is not a trust badge
blocks.label: Common misconception
blocks.body: Free, automated certificates mean a phishing site can have a padlock too. TLS tells you the connection to `examp1e-login.com` is private; it does not tell you `examp1e-login.com` is the bank.

items.q: Who decides which certificate authorities are trusted?
items.a: Browser and operating system makers each keep a root store, a list of authorities that meet their audit rules. An authority that breaks the rules can be removed.
Short lifetimes limit the damage if a key is stolen, and force automation. Public certificates are valid for at most 398 days, and that limit is being cut further.
